title: Lumenworks x Redwood — Quantization Profile Library technical deep dive

body:
Fireflies.ai — Transcript Export

Meeting: Lumenworks x Redwood — Quantization Profile Library technical deep dive
Date: 2025-01-16
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Markus Klein (Solutions Eng), Mateo Alvarez (Serving Runtime), Arjun Desai (Applied ML / Quantization), Jonas Weber (Evals / Perf)
- Lumenworks: Priya Shah (ML Platform), Evan Miller (Staff ML Eng), Rosa Nguyen (SRE), Tom Becker (Security)

Auto-summary (generated)
- Redwood walked through the Quantization Profile Library concept: Redwood-published, versioned quantization variants (fp16/bf16/int8/int4) scoped by model + GPU + kernel constraints.
- Discussed runtime resolution: per-request decision based on model, hardware, and route policy; automatic fallback to baseline on incompatibility.
- Lumenworks emphasized safety for JSON/tool-calling routes and requested clear rollback/monitoring and auditability.
- Monitoring discussed: metrics tagged by profile_id/profile_version and execution mode, plus auto-disable triggers on quality regression.

Topics
- What a “profile” contains (quant method, kernels, calibration notes, constraints)
- Hardware compatibility: A100 vs H100 vs L4, CUDA arch, kernel selection
- Route-level enablement, canaries, precedence/overrides
- Rollback mechanisms and cache invalidation
- Artifact signing/verification and audit logs

Questions captured
- Can we enable int8 for batch summarization but keep interactive chat on bf16?
- What happens if a profile is mis-scoped to the wrong GPU type?
- How do we detect quality regressions specifically for JSON schema compliance?
- In a VPC/private deployment, who signs the artifacts and where is verification enforced?


Transcript

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Markus from Redwood. I’ve got Mateo from runtime, Arjun from applied ML, and Jonas who runs evals and perf gating.

[00:10] Priya Shah: Hey, Priya here. Evan’s on. Rosa from SRE and Tom from security.

[00:15] Markus Klein: Great. Goal today is to go deep on the Quantization Profile Library—what it is, how it’s routed, what’s the blast radius controls, and then the monitoring/rollback story. Not a marketing thing, we can just go straight to the sharp edges.

[00:31] Evan Miller: Perfect. We’ve done some int8 experiments ourselves with, uh, vLLM and a couple kernels. It was… okay until it wasn’t.

[00:40] Mateo Alvarez: (laughs) Yeah. That’s the theme.

[00:43] Markus Klein: Arjun, want to do the two-minute “what is a profile” intro?

[00:47] Arjun Desai: Sure. So when we say “quantization profile” we mean a Redwood-published artifact that’s tied to a specific base model version and a specific quantization approach, like fp16/bf16 baseline, int8 weight-only, int4 weight-only, sometimes activation-aware depending on model family.

[01:06] Arjun Desai: The profile includes the constraints we’ve validated under: GPU class, compute capability, kernel path, and the calibration notes. Not like… a generic ‘turn on int4’ switch. It’s more like “for Llama 3.1 70B, on H100 SXM, with kernel X, use this group size and this packing layout.”

[01:27] Tom Becker: And those are Redwood generated only in v1? Not customer-supplied?

[01:31] Arjun Desai: Correct, in the first release it’s Redwood-published only. That keeps it auditable and consistent with our validation pipeline.

[01:38] Priya Shah: How is it selected? Is it like a header on the request, or…?

[01:42] Markus Klein: Good question. The design we’re shipping is route-level configuration. You enable quantization for a route, optionally with a canary percentage, and then the runtime resolves the best compatible profile per request.

[01:55] Rosa Nguyen: Route-level meaning per endpoint path? Like /v1/chat/completions vs /v1/embeddings?

[02:02] Markus Klein: It’s per Redwood “route” object, which maps to an API surface plus your pinned model and policies. Most customers map routes to workloads, like “interactive_chat_prod” vs “offline_summarization_batch.”

[02:16] Evan Miller: So we can do int8 on offline summarization only. That’s basically what we want.

[02:22] Jonas Weber: And separately, we can keep your JSON/tool-calling route on baseline until we have confidence.

[02:28] Priya Shah: Yeah JSON mode is the scary one. We’ve seen quantization make the model like slightly more… sloppy with braces.

[02:36] Arjun Desai: Exactly. We treat those as different prompt sets and different gates.

[02:41] Mateo Alvarez: Maybe I’ll explain the runtime selection flow, because that’s where the safety comes from.

[02:46] Markus Klein: Please.

[02:47] Mateo Alvarez: So at request time, the runtime has: the resolved base model version, the hardware we’re actually executing on—like A100 80GB versus H100—and also some request characteristics like expected sequence length regime (we bin by context length ranges).

[03:05] Mateo Alvarez: We do a lookup in the model registry for profiles that match (model_id, model_version, quant_mode, gpu_arch, kernel_compat). If the route policy says quantization is enabled, we attempt to choose a profile. If there is no compatible profile, or validation fails, we fall back to baseline.

[03:24] Evan Miller: When you say validation fails, what fails? Like checksum?

[03:28] Mateo Alvarez: Several things: artifact integrity checks (signature), schema version compatibility, and then runtime compatibility checks. Like the kernel expects SM90 but you’re on SM80, or the profile says “requires flash-attn v3 path” and this worker is running a different build.

[03:46] Tom Becker: Signature—who signs? Redwood? And verification happens where?

[03:50] Mateo Alvarez: Redwood signs. Verification happens in the runtime at load time and also in the registry fetch layer. In Private deployments, we can either ship Redwood public key pinned, or if you require customer-controlled signing we can talk about that as an enterprise control. We’re building it with the assumption we need verifiable provenance.

[04:10] Tom Becker: Ok. We can’t accept unsigned artifacts. We’ll need details.

[04:13] Markus Klein: We’ll send the security notes after. It’s in our threat model doc but we can summarize.

[04:18] Rosa Nguyen: I want to ask about the “fall back.” Is it per-request fallback, or does it disable the route?

[04:24] Mateo Alvarez: Both exist depending on why. If it’s just “no profile exists for this GPU,” we do per-request fallback to baseline and emit a metric “quantization_requested_but_unavailable.”

[04:36] Mateo Alvarez: If it’s a hard error like “profile is invalid or fails signature,” we treat that as a configuration issue and we can auto-disable quantization for the route in the control plane depending on policy, because otherwise you could spam logs.

[04:52] Rosa Nguyen: So it can flip a toggle automatically?

[04:55] Markus Klein: That’s part of the rollback tooling. The SRE team wanted an auto-disable hook on regression signals.

[05:01] Priya Shah: What’s considered a regression signal? We can’t just use 5xx, because quality can degrade silently.

[05:07] Jonas Weber: Yeah. We use a combination. For runtime safety: elevated 5xx, elevated fallback rate, timeouts, and perf regression beyond threshold.

[05:18] Jonas Weber: For quality, we have two layers: pre-publish eval gating and post-deploy monitoring. Pre-publish is: we run baseline vs quantized on prompt sets and measure deltas. Post-deploy is trickier—customers can optionally integrate structured output validators and emit “schema invalid” counters.

[05:38] Evan Miller: We do have a JSON schema validator in our app layer.

[05:41] Jonas Weber: Perfect. If you can emit a metric like “json_parse_fail” tagged by route, we can correlate with our quantization execution tags and auto-disable if it spikes.

[05:53] Priya Shah: So your telemetry includes “this request ran quantized”?

[05:56] Mateo Alvarez: Yes. We tag traces and metrics with profile_id, profile_version, execution_mode=baseline|quantized, and kernel_path.

[06:07] Rosa Nguyen: Can we see it in the console per route?

[06:10] Markus Klein: In beta, yes. There’s a route settings panel showing current mode, canary percent, and a link to dashboards. The dashboards show latency p50/p95, tokens/sec, error rate, and a “format compliance” panel if you provide those signals.

[06:28] Evan Miller: Canary percent. Is it like random sampling per request?

[06:32] Mateo Alvarez: It’s deterministic hashing on request id and route, so it’s stable-ish. We didn’t want session flapping too much. But there are caveats for streaming chat; we keep it consistent per request obviously.

[06:46] Priya Shah: We have a “conversation id.” Could we pin by that?

[06:50] Markus Klein: Today it’s by request. For multi-turn “conversation,” we can talk about best practices—often you route by workload anyway. But yeah, we can take that feature request.

[07:02] Arjun Desai: On the quant modes: the thing we’re seeing across model families is int8 tends to be fairly safe for a lot of summarization and even chat, but int4 can be very workload-sensitive, especially tool-calling and structured output.

[07:18] Evan Miller: That matches our experience.

[07:20] Priya Shah: What models are you starting with?

[07:23] Arjun Desai: For beta, it’s a small set: Llama 3.1 8B and 70B variants, and a couple Mistral-family models. We scope by GPU: H100 and A100 first, then L4 where it makes sense.

[07:41] Evan Miller: L4? Like inference on L4 in some regions?

[07:44] Mateo Alvarez: Yeah, mostly cost-sensitive regions. But L4 is more constrained; some kernels don’t support the same fast paths and memory patterns.

[07:53] Rosa Nguyen: So that’s one of the “hardware constraints.” If we’re on Dedicated, can we ensure it’s always A100 only?

[07:59] Markus Klein: Yes. Dedicated pools are fixed SKUs, so your profile availability is more predictable. On Hosted, it depends on routing and capacity, but we won’t run an incompatible profile on a different GPU. Worst case it falls back.

[08:15] Priya Shah: But fallback could change cost unexpectedly.

[08:18] Markus Klein: Totally. We expose a “quantization coverage” metric—how many requests actually ran quantized. It’s important for cost reporting.

[08:27] Jonas Weber: And we can set alerting: if coverage drops below X% for that route, page someone or at least alert.

[08:34] Tom Becker: Audit logs. When someone enables this per route, is there an audit trail?

[08:39] Markus Klein: Yep. Route config changes produce audit log entries: who changed it, old/new values, and whether it was manually disabled or auto-disabled by a policy.

[08:50] Tom Becker: Good. And RBAC on who can enable?

[08:53] Markus Klein: Also yes, it’s a privileged action. Usually “Admin” or “Platform Engineer” role.

[09:00] Evan Miller: Let’s talk about the actual performance improvement. What do you typically see? Like 2x?

[09:06] Arjun Desai: It depends. For int8 weight-only on A100/H100, we typically see 1.2x to 1.6x tokens/sec uplift and cost per token reduction mainly from throughput. For int4, you can get more, but it can be limited by kernel maturity and the workload’s context length.

[09:25] Jonas Weber: Also, long-context changes it. Sometimes the quantized path helps decode but doesn’t help prefill as much, or vice versa.

[09:34] Evan Miller: We care about long context summarization—like 16k to 32k input.

[09:39] Mateo Alvarez: That’s a great example. Prefill dominates at those lengths. Some quant kernels give less win on prefill. Also KV cache behavior matters. You might see improvement but not 2x.

[09:55] Priya Shah: And does quantization affect max context? Like memory usage changes.

[10:00] Mateo Alvarez: It can reduce weight memory, but KV cache is often still fp16/bf16. So you don’t get a linear context increase. Some profiles include “kv_cache_dtype” constraints but we’re conservative there.

[10:15] Rosa Nguyen: If you’re conservative, where’s the risk? Mostly output quality?

[10:20] Arjun Desai: Output quality and also edge-case runtime behavior. Example: a profile scoped incorrectly to GPU arch can cause kernel crash or weird perf. That’s why we pin to hardware constraints.

[10:34] Mateo Alvarez: We had an internal incident (not sure if you saw) where too many workers refreshed profiles at once—cache stampede—and that caused latency spikes. We hotfixed with backoff and rate limit.

[10:47] Rosa Nguyen: That’s exactly what I worry about. How do you invalidate caches?

[10:51] Mateo Alvarez: Profiles are cached with a TTL and also versioned. When a route flips to a new profile version, workers lazily fetch. We added jitter and concurrency caps so you don’t get a thundering herd.

[11:06] Evan Miller: So if you publish v1.2.3 of a profile, the runtime picks it up automatically?

[11:10] Markus Klein: Only if the route is set to “track latest minor” or similar. Most customers pin exact version or do an explicit rollout.

[11:19] Priya Shah: We’d want explicit. Like we control when we move.

[11:22] Markus Klein: That’s the recommended default.

[11:25] Jonas Weber: On the eval side, before we publish a profile, it goes through a gating run. We compare baseline vs quantized on prompt sets: general chat, summarization, and crucially structured output sets.

[11:40] Jonas Weber: We look at pass/fail metrics, sometimes with statistical tests, but in practice we’re looking for “no worse than X” on quality and “at least Y% improvement” on cost/perf for it to be worth it.

[11:55] Evan Miller: What is X? Like 1%?

[11:57] Jonas Weber: It depends by metric. For exact-match structured outputs, any meaningful drop can be unacceptable. For other metrics, we have thresholds—think low single-digit relative regression allowed, but it’s prompt-set specific. For JSON correctness, we’re stricter.

[12:15] Priya Shah: Do you have a dedicated tool-calling eval set? Or is it like generic.

[12:20] Arjun Desai: We’re expanding it. Right now we have a starter set but we’re adding edge cases: nested objects, long tool args, and “JSON mode” style strict formatting.

[12:31] Evan Miller: We can contribute a few prompts.

[12:33] Markus Klein: That would be great, even sanitized. Helps the profile library be safer.

[12:38] Tom Becker: But if we contribute prompts, where do they live? Data retention?

[12:42] Markus Klein: If you send them, we can keep them in a restricted eval bucket with retention rules. Or you can run the eval harness in your environment for Private—depending on deployment.

[12:53] Tom Becker: We’d prefer in our environment.

[12:55] Markus Klein: Understood.

[12:57] Rosa Nguyen: So what’s the rollback story in practice? Say we enable int8 on route A, 10% canary, and we see JSON failures. What happens?

[13:07] Markus Klein: You have three levers: (1) set canary to 0 immediately, (2) disable quantization for the route, (3) pin back to a previous profile version.

[13:18] Markus Klein: If you set canary to 0, traffic goes baseline instantly. There is a propagation delay—seconds to a couple minutes—depending on control plane sync.

[13:27] Mateo Alvarez: Also, the runtime will keep the baseline kernels warm. We don’t unload baseline just because quantization is enabled. So rollback doesn’t require rebuilding.

[13:38] Rosa Nguyen: Good.

[13:39] Evan Miller: Does disabling flush the profile cache? Like you don’t want it to keep trying.

[13:44] Mateo Alvarez: On disable, we stop selecting the profile. The artifact may still be in local cache, but it’s unused. If you suspect corruption, we can force cache flush; there’s an operational endpoint. We try to avoid using it unless needed.

[13:59] Priya Shah: And you said auto-disable exists.

[14:02] Jonas Weber: Yeah. If a metric crosses a threshold—like your “json_parse_fail” rate spikes correlated with quantized execution—we can have a policy that automatically sets canary to 0 and opens an incident event. It’s conservative.

[14:17] Tom Becker: Is that “policy” auditable too?

[14:20] Markus Klein: Yes. Auto actions show as “system actor” with the reason and the triggering signal.

[14:27] Evan Miller: How do we validate cost savings? We need to prove tokens-per-dollar improved.

[14:32] Markus Klein: We have a cost attribution path that tags quantized vs baseline. You can compare same route, same time window, with canary split. That’s the cleanest: canary 10% quantized vs 90% baseline and compare output tokens, latency, and cost.

[14:49] Jonas Weber: Also quality: you can sample outputs and run validators.

[14:54] Priya Shah: We’ll do that.

[14:56] Evan Miller: Let’s ask about kernel constraints. Mateo, when does it break? We’ve seen weird issues on A10 and L4.

[15:05] Mateo Alvarez: Yeah. The two big categories are (a) compute capability differences (SM80 vs SM90) and (b) driver/CUDA stack differences.

[15:14] Mateo Alvarez: Some int4 kernels are only implemented for SM90 right now. If you’re on A100 (SM80), we might have an int8 profile but not int4. Or the int4 path exists but performance is not good enough to justify.

[15:29] Evan Miller: So you could say “route wants int4” but you only deliver int8.

[15:33] Markus Klein: We don’t silently downgrade quant mode. If you say “int4 only,” we either find an int4 profile or we run baseline and we tell you coverage is 0%.

[15:43] Priya Shah: That’s good. No surprises.

[15:46] Arjun Desai: The profile metadata explicitly lists supported quant_modes and supported hardware. That’s important.

[15:53] Tom Becker: Is there any chance it runs a profile on the wrong hardware? Like mislabel.

[15:58] Mateo Alvarez: That’s the “mis-scoped profile” risk. We mitigate with multiple checks: the profile declares gpu_arch and also we check the kernel’s compiled target and some runtime sanity checks. If mismatch, we log and fall back.

[16:14] Rosa Nguyen: In the incident you mentioned, what happened? Just for learning.

[16:18] Mateo Alvarez: In one case, a profile manifest had an overly broad hardware selector and it got considered “compatible” for a GPU class where the kernel behaved poorly and increased errors. We tightened the schema and added more strict matching. That’s why we’re insisting on explicit scoping.

[16:38] Priya Shah: Makes sense.

[16:40] Jonas Weber: Also why we’re making it opt-in. We’re not turning it on globally without customer control.

[16:47] Evan Miller: Okay. For us, the plan would be: enable int8 on batch summarization route with canary. Keep chat baseline. And never enable int4 until we’re really confident.

[16:59] Markus Klein: That’s the typical safe path.

[17:02] Priya Shah: What about dedicated vs hosted. We’re leaning dedicated for predictability.

[17:07] Markus Klein: Dedicated makes the hardware matrix simpler. You pick, say, A100 80GB. Then we can tell you exactly which profiles exist. Hosted is more dynamic, still safe but less deterministic for coverage.

[17:20] Evan Miller: And private/VPC? We might need VPC later.

[17:24] Markus Klein: Same config surface. The profile library artifacts are distributed through the model registry; private control plane can fetch them through your allowed network path.

[17:34] Tom Becker: Network path and artifact access—least privilege. Can the runtime fetch only the profiles it needs?

[17:41] Mateo Alvarez: Yes. Tokens are scoped by org and by model permissions. And we can further scope by environment. But exact policy depends on your deployment mode.

[17:52] Tom Becker: Ok.

[17:54] Rosa Nguyen: Observability—do we get a dashboard with “quantized vs baseline”? Or do we need to build it.

[18:00] Markus Klein: We have a built-in dashboard. It’s split by route and can filter by profile_id/version. It shows latency, throughput, error rate, fallback rate, and cost per 1K tokens. You can also export to your own Grafana via our metrics sink.

[18:18] Rosa Nguyen: And alerts? Pre-canned?

[18:20] Markus Klein: There are suggested alerts: error rate delta, latency delta, quant coverage drop, and any “profile incompatibility” spikes. For quality alerts, we need your app signal.

[18:33] Priya Shah: We can provide that.

[18:35] Evan Miller: On quality: do you do like “LLM-as-a-judge” to compare baseline vs quantized?

[18:42] Jonas Weber: Sometimes. For summarization, we do model-graded metrics plus some task-specific heuristics. But for structured outputs we prefer deterministic validators.

[18:54] Priya Shah: Same. We don’t trust judge models for JSON validity.

[18:58] Arjun Desai: Another thing: we attach eval results to the profile publication so you can inspect what prompt sets it passed, what regressions exist, and any known limitations.

[19:12] Evan Miller: Like a report card.

[19:13] Arjun Desai: Exactly.

[19:15] Markus Klein: We can show those in the console too over time.

[19:18] Priya Shah: That’s helpful.

[19:20] Evan Miller: I want to dig into “calibration notes.” What does that mean in practice?

[19:25] Arjun Desai: For int4 especially, you often need some calibration dataset or method. The profile includes how it was calibrated—like which prompt set or a representative dataset—and any caveats like “works best on summarization and chat; tool-calling shows occasional formatting drift.”

[19:42] Evan Miller: So it’s not like you calibrate on our data.

[19:45] Arjun Desai: Not unless we do a custom engagement. The library is Redwood-published with generic-but-representative calibration.

[19:54] Priya Shah: That’s fine. We’ll treat it as “best effort.”

[19:57] Markus Klein: Right, and the route-level canary is your safety net.

[20:01] Rosa Nguyen: Can we do per-customer overrides? We have multiple tenants.

[20:06] Markus Klein: There’s a concept of org-level default and route-level. Customer-level overrides are planned; in beta we can do it for some enterprise accounts, but I don’t want to promise general availability.

[20:19] Rosa Nguyen: Ok. We can also create separate routes per tenant if needed.

[20:23] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[20:25] Tom Becker: Any deprecation policy? Like if you publish a profile, do you ever pull it?

[20:31] Arjun Desai: We can revoke if it’s unsafe. It’s versioned and signed. We can mark it as deprecated and prevent new enablements while leaving existing pinned versions running if needed, but with warnings. If it’s a security issue we can force disable.

[20:48] Tom Becker: Okay.

[20:49] Evan Miller: How fast does a config change propagate? If we disable, is it minutes?

[20:55] Mateo Alvarez: It’s typically under a minute, but worst case a couple minutes depending on control plane propagation and worker polling interval.

[21:03] Rosa Nguyen: That’s acceptable if alerts are fast.

[21:06] Jonas Weber: For auto-disable, we’re targeting near real-time based on metrics windows. Still, there’s always lag.

[21:14] Priya Shah: That’s why we’d start with 1% canary.

[21:17] Markus Klein: Yup.

[21:19] Evan Miller: On long context: we saw quantization help decode but prefill got slower. Any reason?

[21:26] Mateo Alvarez: It can happen if the quantized kernel has overhead in prefill, or if it doesn’t fuse operations as well. Also memory bandwidth patterns change. That’s why we benchmark across sequence length bins.

[21:41] Jonas Weber: Our perf suite runs separate bins: short prompts, medium, long context. We track p50/p95 latency and tokens/sec.

[21:52] Priya Shah: Do you share those perf results with customers?

[21:55] Markus Klein: For the profiles you’re using, yes, we can share summary results and the conditions. It’s not always 1:1 with your workload, but it’s a baseline.

[22:06] Evan Miller: Okay.

[22:08] Tom Becker: One more security question. If someone compromises the registry, could they push a malicious profile?

[22:15] Mateo Alvarez: They’d need signing keys. Our publish path is permissioned and keys are protected; runtime verifies signatures. Without the private key, you can’t produce a valid artifact. Also audit logs on publish.

[22:30] Tom Becker: Good.

[22:31] Markus Klein: We can include the threat model doc in the follow-up.

[22:35] Priya Shah: Switching gears: how do we get into the beta?

[22:39] Markus Klein: We’ll take this as part of your technical evaluation. Next step is we pick 1-2 routes, define success criteria (cost drop, latency, and no quality regressions), and then we enable int8 at low canary.

[22:55] Priya Shah: Success criteria: we want ~20% cost reduction on that route without increasing JSON failures. And no SLO breach.

[23:04] Rosa Nguyen: Specifically p95 latency cannot exceed baseline by more than, say, 5%.

[23:09] Markus Klein: Great. That’s concrete.

[23:12] Jonas Weber: For quality, we can define a threshold: JSON parse failure rate must not increase beyond X per thousand requests. You can set it.

[23:21] Evan Miller: We can set X. Probably basically zero. Maybe allow tiny.

[23:25] Priya Shah: For summarization, it’s not strict JSON though. That route is free-form.

[23:30] Evan Miller: Yeah batch summarization is plain text. So quality gating there is more like human review + some heuristics.

[23:37] Jonas Weber: Perfect. That route is a good first candidate.

[23:41] Arjun Desai: For summarization, int8 is usually safe. Tool-calling we’ll be more careful.

[23:47] Markus Klein: Are you currently pinned to a specific model?

[23:50] Priya Shah: We use Llama 3.1 70B mostly, and a smaller one for some routes.

[23:56] Markus Klein: Great. That aligns.

[23:59] Evan Miller: We tried AWS endpoints and the cost is just… yeah. Not great.

[24:03] Markus Klein: Understood.

[24:05] Rosa Nguyen: Also, we’re nervous about “silent quality issues.” Is there any Redwood-side monitoring for “output distribution drift” or something?

[24:13] Jonas Weber: We’re experimenting with proxy signals like refusal rate changes, length distribution changes, and “stop reason” distribution. Those can be early indicators. But they’re not perfect.

[24:26] Evan Miller: Output length changes is real. We saw int4 sometimes got shorter.

[24:30] Arjun Desai: Yes. We include length deltas in eval reports.

[24:34] Markus Klein: And at runtime, we can show tokens out per request; if it shifts, you’ll see it.

[24:40] Priya Shah: Ok.

[24:42] Markus Klein: I think we’ve hit most topics. Any other deep dive questions before we do next steps?

[24:49] Tom Becker: Just confirming: in VPC/private, we can restrict who can enable quantization and see audit logs.

[24:55] Markus Klein: Yes.

[24:56] Rosa Nguyen: And rollback is immediate enough.

[24:59] Mateo Alvarez: And baseline path is always available; fallback happens automatically on incompatibility.

[25:05] Evan Miller: Can we request to see a sample profile manifest? Like what fields.

[25:10] Arjun Desai: Yes, we can share an example with some fields redacted if needed.

[25:14] Jonas Weber: And we can share the “report card” format for eval results.

[25:18] Markus Klein: Perfect. Here’s what I’ll do: I’ll email a short recap, sample config for route enablement, and the security/threat model overview. Mateo will share the GPU compatibility notes. Arjun/Jonas will propose an eval plan for your two candidate routes.

[25:35] Priya Shah: Sounds good.

[25:37] Markus Klein: Evan/Priya, if you can send a rough traffic shape—QPS, input lengths, max output—and any validators you have, that’ll help us size and set alerts.

[25:47] Evan Miller: Yep.

[25:48] Rosa Nguyen: I’ll send what we have for SLOs and the alerting windows.

[25:52] Markus Klein: Great. We’ll schedule a follow-up in about a week to review the plan and maybe start the canary.

[26:00] Priya Shah: Works.

[26:01] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

[26:03] (Call continues with light scheduling / goodbyes; transcript ends early due to recording stop)

— End of transcript —
